title: Hugo Spritz
steps: Fill a large wine glass or stemless glass with ice.
Muddle the mint leaves together with a squeeze of lime in the glass.
Pour in the St-Germain, then the Prosecco.
Top with San Pellegrino and give it one gentle stir (don't overmix — keep the bubbles).
Garnish with a lime wheel and a fresh mint sprig.

sections.heading: Chasing the Shade on an Atlanta Afternoon
sections.body: There's a particular kind of heat that settles over an Atlanta patio in the late afternoon — thick and unmoving, the kind that flattens every ambition down to just staying in the shade with something cold in hand. That's the mood I was in when I started craving a drink that felt less like a treat and more like relief: something bright, effervescent, and just sweet enough to make the humidity bearable.

sections.heading: A Taste of Sicily, Rediscovered
sections.body: My mind went straight back to a trip years ago, sitting at a little table along the Sicilian coast as the sun dipped low over the water. Someone nearby was sipping something pale gold and fizzing, garnished with mint and a curl of lime, and I couldn't help but ask what it was. A Hugo Spritz, they told me — prosecco, elderflower liqueur, and a splash of sparkling water, finished with whatever herbs happened to be on hand that day. It tasted like the whole afternoon distilled into a glass: light, floral, and completely unhurried.

sections.heading: Bringing the Patio Back to Life
sections.body: Back home, with the Atlanta sun doing its best impression of a Sicilian summer, I wanted to recreate that exact feeling — a drink to sip slowly while the ice loses its fight against the heat. San Pellegrino brings back a little of that Italian sparkle, and muddling the mint with a squeeze of lime gives it just enough brightness to cut through the sweetness of the elderflower. It's become my go-to for these long, hot afternoons — proof that some of the best souvenirs aren't things you pack in a suitcase, but flavors you carry home and recreate, one spritz at a time.
